claims.text: As-cast HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure containing nano-precipitates, distinct grain boundaries, and varied interface characters.
An ML model trained on quantitative microstructural features can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
Relevant input features include grain-size distributions, interface characteristics, and nano-precipitate morphology.
The proposed ML model will be more accurate than established multiscale simulation methods.
The proposed ML model will provide more than a tenfold reduction in prediction time relative to conventional simulations.
Feature-selection and ensemble-learning methods can improve predictive performance and interpretability for HEA mechanical-property models.
The hierarchical heterostructure contains distinct phases, grain boundaries, and nano-precipitates.
The heterostructural constituents mediate solid-solution, grain-boundary, and precipitation strengthening.
Physics-informed microstructural features can capture contributions from strengthening mechanisms.
The selected microstructural features can capture internal stress concentrators relevant to fracture behavior.
Microstructural features can serve as a rapid proxy for detailed atomistic or continuum states.
ICME approaches can integrate CALPHAD phase prediction with ML-based phase and property prediction modules.
Established computational methods can require many CPU hours.
Conventional simulations do not fully capture the effects of hierarchical microstructural details in HfNbTiVAl10.
The model may fail when the extracted features incompletely represent the material’s microstructural complexity.
The model may fail when the hierarchical structure evolves under testing conditions outside the training regime.
Insufficient coverage of HfNbTiVAl10 microstructural variation in the training dataset may limit model robustness.
ML is a relatively quick and cost-effective approach for identifying patterns and predicting mechanical or elastic properties in high-entropy and refractory complex concentrated alloys.
A statistically significant error reduction exceeding a preset 10% threshold is the proposed minimum accuracy improvement.
Simultaneous failure to achieve a tenfold speedup and the preset accuracy improvement would decisively falsify the hypothesis.
